editorialNotes.short: Beyoncé opens the vault to celebrate her second solo album’s 20th b’day.
editorialNotes.standard: After the 2003 release of Dangerously in Love, her chart-topping, award-winning solo debut, Beyoncé was, in a word, busy—with wrapping up her work with Destiny’s Child, the trio that launched her career; with her first tour on her own, which had her headlining London’s Wembley Stadium; but also with her crossover success in movies, as she booked starring roles in and filmed The Pink Panther and Dreamgirls. When she eventually made it back into the studio, she convened an all-star lineup of producers, including Swizz Beatz, The Neptunes, Darkchild and more, and built on the momentum of Dangerously in Love by recording its follow-up in less than a month. Given the resulting hits of B’Day—which was, indeed, released on 4 September, Beyoncé‘s birthday—it’s easy to see why. She was inspired in the midst of the most prolific artistic stretch of her life to date, and she was eager to push the creative envelope as far as she could. B’Day’s singles have sharper teeth than their predecessors, from “Upgrade U”, the second JAŸ-Z collaboration on the album (the first being the smitten “Deja Vu”), to the vengeful and explosive “Ring the Alarm” and the bittersweet “Irreplaceable”, which rewrote the script on post-breakup independence. The galloping beat of “Get Me Bodied” and discordant melody of “Freakum Dress” remain some of the most recognisable sounds in Beyoncé’s catalogue. Subsequent editions of B’Day featured “Beautiful Liar”, her smouldering duet with Shakira, as well as Spanish versions of “Irreplaceable” and “Listen”, her original, traditional ballad for the Dreamgirls soundtrack. But the 20th-anniversary edition of B’Day offers up the largest haul yet from the depths of Queen Bey’s vault. Outtakes and deep cuts abound, like “MORNING DEW (DONK)”, Pharrell collaboration “CAN I WATCH YOU” and “CREOLE”, a single that was included on international variants of the original deluxe. The 31-song tracklist also includes one-off singles (like “CHECK ON IT”, her smash from the Pink Panther soundtrack) and “CUERPO (TUMBAO)”, a vibrant Latin update of “Get Me Bodied” that not only features a sample from salsa queen Celia Cruz’s “La Negra Tiene Tumbao”, but also an appearance from Maluma. At the end of the track, Bey jokes that her “Spanish is not very good lookin’”—but we disagree. Additional Spanish reworks of B’Day standards, such as “Get Me Bodied” (or “Mueve el Cuerpo”) and an unforgettable version of “Irreplaceable”, “IRREEMPLAZABLE (COMO LA FLOR)”, featuring a seamless tie-in of the late tejano star Selena’s “Como La Flor”, abound as well. It’s a B’Day gift two decades in the making.

editorialNotes.short: The album that inspired a generation of ripped-jeans rockers to pick up their first real six-string.
editorialNotes.standard: Bryan Adams' fourth album, Reckless, is so overstuffed with classic-rock-radio perennials, it practically qualifies as a greatest-hits collection. Arena-ready anthems like “Summer of ’69” and “Somebody” stayed true to Adams’ rocker roots, but the simmering intensity of “Run to You”, the lighter-sparking “Heaven” and the soul-powered Tina Turner duet “It’s Only Love” revealed a greater depth to his denim-and-leather image.

editorialNotes.short: Beyoncé and friends pay tribute to everything the light touches.
editorialNotes.standard:
In the lead-up to the release of The Lion King: The Gift, a collection of music inspired by the 2019 reboot of the classic Disney film, Beyoncé remarked that the project was meant to be “a love letter to Africa”. As executive producer, Bey made it a point to solicit contributions from artists spanning a number of the continent’s many culturally rich traditions and regions, including Nigeria, Ghana, Cameroon and South Africa. The album, in fact, is a separate project from the film’s official soundtrack, but that doesn’t stop Beyoncé and a cohort of hand-selected talents from telling that timeless story of the Pride Lands through song.
Not unlike the film, The Gift chronicles a saga of personal growth, filtered through some of the brightest stars in Afrobeats and Afrofusion. Artists like Mr Eazi, Yemi Alade, Burna Boy, Tiwa Savage and Tekno sing in multiple languages about embracing blessings (“JA ARA E”), staying the path (“DON’T JEALOUS ME”) and rising into your own majesty (“KEYS TO THE KINGDOM”). Family is a constant theme, with Beyoncé singing to her children directly on “BIGGER” and then about her father on “FIND YOUR WAY BACK". She’s procured contributions from some of her favourite US-born MCs, like Kendrick Lamar, co-star Childish Gambino, Tierra Whack and, of course, the man co-captaining her household, JAŸ-Z. The Gift, then, is a compilation of talents both African and Afro-diasporic strong enough to buttress the throne of the woman we’ve come to know as Queen Bey.
